planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Minor forms a tidy mound well suited to a mixed border or small-space planting.

directions: Pink Minor is a compact dwarf deutzia whose teardrop-shaped, purplish-pink buds open into starry, inch-wide white flowers that hang thickly along softly arching branches in mid-spring, giving a two-tone pink-and-white effect as buds and open blooms mingle. New stems emerge a warm coppery color and mature to dark green, providing subtle contrast even after bloom finishes. Its low, dense, naturally rounded habit fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller gardens where full-size deutzia would overwhelm the space, and the fragrant flowers draw bees and butterflies. Since it blooms on the prior year's wood, prune only right after flowering to avoid cutting off next season's buds; established plants tolerate average garden soil with little fuss.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; foliage color develops most brightly with full-day sun exposure.

directions: Dream Catcher stands apart from the species and from the older 'Pink Cloud' selection through its constantly shifting foliage color, emerging bright gold with bronze-copper tips in spring, softening to yellow-chartreuse through summer, and finishing with a golden-orange fall display, all set off by clusters of soft pink, bell-shaped flowers along arching branches in late spring. Its broad, fountain-like habit and tolerance for dry shade and drought once established make it a low-maintenance choice for a mixed border or naturalized planting where season-long foliage color matters as much as the spring bloom. Deer generally leave it alone. Prune immediately after flowering, thinning some of the oldest canes at ground level to keep the shrub renewed and full from the base.

common_name: Snowbelle Mock Orange (Compact Double-Flowered Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Snowbelle's compact size suits foundation plantings and smaller gardens where full-size mock orange would be too large.

directions: Snowbelle packs the classic mock orange experience into a tidy, low-growing frame, smothering itself in large, fully double, pure white flowers in late spring that carry the same intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance as full-size selections. Its compact, rounded habit and good heat and cold tolerance make it a reliable choice for hedges, low screens, borders, and foundation plantings where taller mock orange cultivars would quickly outgrow the space. Best flowering and fragrance come with full sun, though it tolerates part shade. Prune right after flowering since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and expect only light annual shaping to keep the naturally dense form neat.

common_name: Miniature Snowflake Mock Orange (Dwarf Double-Flowered Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf sport of Minnesota Snowflake shares its parent's cold hardiness in a much smaller frame.

directions: Discovered as a naturally occurring dwarf branch sport of the cold-hardy Minnesota Snowflake, this compact selection produces the same profuse clusters of fragrant, double white flowers in late spring but stays only two to three feet tall, making it far better suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, and mixed borders than its larger parent. The dense branching habit is clothed in glossy dark green foliage that stays clean through the season, and the intense sweet orange-blossom scent carries just as strongly as on full-size mock orange cultivars. It shares its parent's excellent cold hardiness and disease resistance. Prune immediately after flowering, since buds for next year's bloom form on the current season's growth.

common_name: Illuminati Arch Mock Orange (Rugged-Foliage Arching Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a minimum of six hours of direct sun brings the heaviest, most fragrant bloom.

directions: Illuminati Arch was bred to fix the biggest complaint about mock orange — ratty, thin, tattered-looking summer foliage — by pairing the classic cascades of sweetly fragrant white spring flowers with thick, glossy, rugged leaves that stay deep green and attractive all season long. Its gracefully arching, compact habit fits mixed borders and foundation plantings at a more manageable scale than older mock orange cultivars, without sacrificing the intense old-fashioned orange-blossom fragrance the genus is prized for. It tolerates part shade but flowers and perfumes the garden most heavily with a half-day or more of direct sun. Prune immediately after flowering, since it blooms on the prior year's wood and needs little other routine care once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color and bloom are both strongest with at least six hours of direct sun.

directions: Shining Sensation emerges each spring with coppery-bronze new growth that matures into glossy, deep burgundy foliage with a distinctive sheen not seen on most dark-leaved weigela, holding its rich color well through summer heat. In late spring it produces a heavy flush of pink, trumpet-shaped flowers with contrasting buttery-yellow anthers that draw hummingbirds, with a scattering of repeat bloom into summer. Its dense, mounded, multi-stemmed habit fills a medium-sized spot in a mixed border or foundation planting without staking or heavy maintenance. Prune right after the main spring bloom to shape, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood and later cuts sacrifice next year's display.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; the heaviest tricolor bloom display develops with a full day of direct sun.

directions: Czechmark Trilogy produces an unusual three-color bloom display in a single late-spring flush, with funnel-shaped flowers opening white, aging to soft pink, and finally deepening to rich red, so that white, pink, and red blooms all appear together on the shrub at once for a lively, multicolored effect. Unlike the Sonic Bloom series, which spreads its color over repeated summer flushes, Czechmark Trilogy concentrates its display into one spectacular spring show with only light scattered rebloom afterward. Its compact, rounded habit stays tidy in a mixed border or foundation planting, tolerates a range of soils, and shrugs off deer and rabbit browsing better than most flowering shrubs. Prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage veining contrast is most pronounced with full-day sun.

directions: Dark Horse stands out among dark-leaved weigela for its distinctive dark bronze foliage traced with contrasting lime-green venation, a marbled effect that provides season-long visual interest even between bloom cycles. In late spring the shrub produces a heavy flush of purplish-pink, tubular flowers that draw hummingbirds and contrast strikingly against the patterned foliage. Its neat, compact, low-spreading habit needs minimal upkeep and fits well as an accent plant or in a shrub border at a smaller scale than many older weigela cultivars. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to maintain shape, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood and later pruning removes next year's display.
